First touch Receive with a purpose. Take the first touch towards a useful space, ready for the next action. Where does the ball go when she receives? Can she see a way to keep it away from pressure? Receive passes from different angles. Try a touch across the body or into space, then add a defender when she is ready. In her next game, look for an opportunity to receive away from an opponent and keep the next pass available. Ask which touch helped her keep the ball. Look at direction and control, then decide whether to repeat or change the challenge. Where could your first touch take you? Looking before receiving See the picture earlier. Look before the ball arrives to understand the space, teammates and pressure nearby. When does she look around? What information does she use before choosing her next action? Build in a reason to look: a teammate moves, a passing option changes or a defender closes a space. Give her time to notice and respond. Try a look over the shoulder before receiving in a suitable moment, then use what she has seen to make her decision. Ask what she noticed and whether it changed her choice. Adjust the pace and pressure to keep the task useful. What can you find out before it arrives? Beating a defender Create a way past. Recognise when to take on a defender and use a change of direction or speed to get beyond her. How does she approach an opponent? Can she spot space to attack or a better passing option? Start with a manageable one-to-one challenge. Explore a feint, a change of direction and an acceleration into space. Look for a suitable one-to-one moment in a game. Decide whether to dribble, combine with a teammate or keep possession. Discuss what the defender did and which action created space. Progress can include choosing a useful pass. PERSONAL SUPPORT. Here for her football. Here for her. Getting to know a player matters as much as getting to know her game. FOUNDER & HEAD COACH Dean Parkinson Helping each player understand her game and find her next step. Dean created STAR to give girls more individual attention and a clear focus for their football. He starts by listening to what each player enjoys, what she finds difficult and what she wants to achieve. His seven years of coaching experience span women’s football, youth football, individual development and goalkeeper coaching. He is also Head Coach of Staplegrove Ladies. As Player Welfare Officer, Becky listens to players’ concerns and helps them communicate what they need. She draws on her experience as a parent of children with special educational needs, offering patience, reassurance and time to settle in. Email Becky Louise Lock Building the foundations for players to feel confident with the ball. The referral does not create a STAR account or subscribe you to marketing. The website does not save the referral to the player database; copies remain in the email delivery and club email systems. For questions about the club’s use or retention of your referral, contact the club at that address. You can contact STAR about its handling of the referral using the details above. Private player onboarding Signed-in parents and players can save a player’s identity and contact details, football experience, goals, support needs, relevant health and emergency arrangements, training-top size, boot size and availability. STAR uses this information to understand the player, arrange her free assessment and plan suitable coaching. Share information relevant to participation; you may ask to discuss sensitive matters privately. Drafts are saved when you choose Save progress. Access is restricted to the account that created the profile, the separately linked parent and player accounts, and authorised STAR managers. A separate player login can be linked later; it is not needed for the parent to submit the form or request an assessment. An optional account-link invitation is restricted to the recipient’s verified email and expires after 48 hours. Completing onboarding does not grant access to another player’s existing coaching records. Identification photograph The head-to-toe photograph is used to identify the player and for her private profile. Upload a recent photograph in ordinary clothing or training kit. Photographs are converted to JPEG and location metadata is removed before upload. Identification photographs are stored privately and are not published on the public website by this onboarding process. Participation and media choices The parent or guardian reviews the completed profile and confirms participation in the free assessment. Private coaching photographs/video, public photographs, public video and use of the player’s first name each have separate choices. No promotional choice is selected by default. Declining these media permissions does not prevent an assessment request. Changes to the saved profile require a fresh parent review. Update media choices here and contact STAR about withdrawing permission or removing material already published. If information should no longer be used, contact STAR so the request can be reviewed and the appropriate records corrected or removed. Storage and account security The website is hosted on Vercel. Accounts, onboarding records and private photographs use Supabase; the STAR database project is in its London region. These providers process information to operate the service. Medical details and photographs are not sent through public enquiry emails by the onboarding process. Keeping information accurate and handling requests Tell STAR about changes to health, emergency arrangements or contact details before participation. Contact STAR to request access, correction, deletion, withdrawal of consent or information about how long particular records are kept. Some records may need to be retained for safeguarding or other applicable obligations; STAR will explain any reason a request cannot be met in full. You can also raise a data-protection concern with the Information Commissioner’s Office Safeguarding concerns Onboarding and general messages are not an emergency reporting service. Contact STAR directly about concerns requiring prompt attention. In an immediate emergency call 999.
